findings.element: Medinet Habu: the palace behind the Window of Appearances
findings.description: Ramesses III's ceremonial palace was mudbrick and stood beside the temple's first court. It was joined to that court by a Window of Appearances in the court's south wall, 'between the fourth and fifth columns'. Courtiers and ambassadors gathered in the court below. The king climbed an inner stair to the window, stood above the crowd and threw down rewards. The palace behind it had a 16-column antechamber (the window) and a 4-column audience hall with a throne dais. A second phase added an upper storey. The Harris Papyrus calls the window 'fine gold'. This is exactly the relationship the map needs: a court whose far wall holds the royal window, seen from the court floor.

findings.element: Medinet Habu: religious and captive details around the window
findings.description: A cavetto cornice with a row of carved cobras (uraeus frieze) ran above the window. Below it was a row of projecting heads of twenty foreign captives. The court belongs to a mortuary temple, with Osirid colossi on one side. Leave out the cobras, the Osirid statues and anything temple-related. The captive heads are royal propaganda rather than cult imagery, but they are violent; skipping them is recommended.

findings.element: The Egyptian 'castle': Medinet Habu's migdol gate and enclosure
findings.description: This is the closest Egyptian equivalent to thundah's castle. The precinct is enclosed by a mudbrick wall 315 x 210 m, 18 m high and 10 m thick. The gatehouse is a 'migdol' modelled on Syrian fortresses: two crenellated towers about 22 m high, with the gateway between them. A crenellated stone wall about 4 m high stood in front. A glossary calls half-circle merlons 'Egyptian merlons' and names Medinet Habu as the example. Buhen (Middle Kingdom) is the earliest confirmed fortress with battlements: mudbrick walls about 10 m high and 5 m thick, with towers at intervals. Usable motifs: rounded merlons on a wall top, a pair of battered towers. Both are secular and military.

findings.element: Amarna Great Palace: Broad Court and the projecting window terrace
findings.description: The entrance opened into a court about 160 m square. Its east and west sides were lined with rows of royal statues, many of them granite colossi of the king. A deep columned portico ran across the back of the court, with a central projecting terrace four columns deep. The Window of Appearance probably stood there. The state apartments also had a sunken garden with a row of small chambers on each side. The building was finished with faience mouldings and tiles, hard-stone inlaid hieroglyphs, and inlaid, gilded columns in plant forms. It stood on gypsum foundations that kept the plan. Idea to borrow: set the palace front back so the window reads as a projecting bay at the centre of a long palace front.

findings.element: Amarna: religious imagery in the palaces and window scenes
findings.description: The Broad Court colossi of Akhenaten are described as Osirid (Osiris pose). Some column shafts show the king and queen making offerings to the god. Tomb scenes of the Window of Appearance (e.g. Parennefer, Amarna Tomb 7) show the Aten sun disc with rays above the royal couple. Leave out all of these: statues in Osirid pose, offering scenes, and the Aten disc and rays.

findings.element: Painted pavements (Amarna Great Palace, Maru-Aten)
findings.description: The floors were gypsum plaster painted with nature scenes. In the Great Palace pavement, a central path of bound foreign captives, meant to be trodden underfoot, divided the scene. On each side was a pond with fish and water-lilies and birds fluttering over it, framed by marshes of waving papyrus with wildfowl. A Maru-Aten floor fragment in Cairo shows ducks flying over tufts of reeds and papyrus among floating leaves. The pond, papyrus and ducks are secular. Maru-Aten itself was a sacred precinct (the floor motif is not). The captive path is political rather than religious; skip it.

findings.element: Amarna North Palace: courts and garden court
findings.description: An isolated rectangular palace facing west to the river, built in sections around an open space, symmetrical on an east-west axis. The entrance is through the west façade between two short pylons. The main inner court holds a large depression, rectangular at ground level, now read as a deep well, with a row of tree pits along its north side. A limestone conduit carried its water to a sunken garden court in the north-east corner. That garden was divided by mud ridges into cubit-sized plots, surrounded by small rooms with windows onto it, and ringed with limestone pillar bases. The walls of the 'Green Room' carry a continuous marsh painting: waterfowl, papyrus, and a lotus channel between black silt banks. There was also a many-columned hall whose central columns were spaced wider to carry a raised roof. The altar court with its offering tables is religious; leave it out.

findings.element: Malqata (Amenhotep III): a whitewashed palace with red columns and a painted pool floor
findings.description: Mudbrick, with many bricks stamped with the king's cartouche. Walls were plastered and painted bright white outside, richly coloured inside. The King's Palace covers more than 150 x 100 m and is roughly symmetrical around a central court. The central columned hall (about 50 x 25 m with the royal rooms) has two rows of columns: wooden shafts, probably painted red, on round limestone bases, with papyrus-cluster or lily capitals and clerestory lighting. Wooden columns beside the throne were painted in alternating coloured bands. The floor of the central hall was painted as a pool on the main axis, full of plants and fish with ducks, with reed and papyrus thickets. Ceilings had running spirals with rosettes. A large pleasure lake and gardens lay outside, and the Birket Habu harbour nearby. Stone was used only for column bases, lintels and some floors.

findings.element: Malqata: vulture ceilings
findings.description: The royal bedchamber ceiling showed the goddess Nekhbet. In the reconstruction, the central aisle of the columned hall is covered by a succession of winged vultures. Both are religious; leave them out. The ceiling's alternating ox skulls (bucrania) are an Aegean-style ornament, safer to skip too.

findings.element: Deir el-Ballas North Palace
findings.description: A late 17th-Dynasty campaign palace. It has columned courts and a long entrance corridor grouped around an elevated central platform on casemate foundations (up to about 5 m preserved). The platform carried the raised royal rooms and made the palace look like a fortified 'migdol' tower. Arnold puts it in an enclosure of 156 x 303 m. Walls and floors were painted as pools of fish and tracts of flowering shrubs. It is a precedent for a palace with a raised royal block and a fortress-like silhouette, which fits the castle idea.

findings.element: Merenptah's palace at Memphis: throne room columns and colours
findings.description: The throne room was about 60 x 40 ft, with six white limestone columns about 26 ft high carrying papyrus capitals. Their bases had eight petals in low relief, alternately blue and gold, and the top bands also alternated blue and gold. The walls were mudbrick with fine white stucco. A dado of red and blue niches framed papyrus and lotus bunches on yellow fields. The brick floor was white stucco with colour designs. Door frames and window slabs were limestone. It is a good palette source: white stucco, limestone, and blue, gold and red bands.

findings.element: Merenptah's palace: religious details
findings.description: Mid-shaft reliefs show religious ceremonies. The cartouche rows are interspersed with ankh signs, and the ceiling is blue with yellow stars (a sky ceiling). Leave out all three.

findings.element: Palm column proportions
findings.description: Sahure's granite palm column: originally about 6.45-6.65 m tall, 0.86 m across at the foot (about 7.5 diameters). The capital is 1.68 m tall (about 26% of the height), with nine fronds showing a central rib and fine ripples. Five rope bands sit under the capital, and the abacus is 0.87 m wide (about 1 diameter). Unas's column is 6.60 m tall and 0.87 m across. Palm columns came back into use under Amenhotep III. Karnak's great papyrus columns are about 6-7 diameters high. There is no written Egyptian canon for proportions or spacing. Columns were set close together because stone architraves span little, and wider capitals allowed slightly wider spacing. (These two columns come from pyramid temples, but the palm column is an architectural form, not a cult symbol.)

findings.element: Palace and house columns: wood on stone bases, painted and gilded
findings.description: Stone columns were used only in public buildings. Houses, and even the king's private residence, used wooden columns on stone bases a little more than twice the shaft's diameter. One large Amarna residence had 1.2 m bases, so its shafts were about 0.5-0.6 m across (my estimate). The shafts were plastered and usually painted reddish brown. The Amarna palace capitals were palm-frond forms, with coloured glaze inlays in the ribs and leaves and gilding on the stone around them. Where they would not be seen, red and blue paint replaced the inlays and yellow replaced the gold. Central halls had taller middle aisles with clerestories.

findings.element: Garden court layout: pool and rows of trees
findings.description: The standard garden has a rectangular pool in the centre, with fish, lotus and flowering edges. It is surrounded by rows of trees (sycamore fig, date palm, doum palm, pomegranate) alternating with flower beds. Pools had sloping sides with steps on one side, and vine pergolas gave shade. At Amarna the trees were planted in pits of humus with a round coping. The Nebamun painting (British Museum EA37983) shows a rectangular pool from above with three rows of trees round it, tilapia, ducks, lotus and papyrus. The King's House at Amarna had a court with rows of trees forming an avenue from its pylon entrance. The lotus has rebirth symbolism, but as a garden plant or capital it is ordinary decoration.

findings.element: Garden religious elements
findings.description: The Nebamun pool includes a tree goddess (Nut or Hathor) offering fruit, and a speaking sycamore. Sycamores were the sacred 'tree of life'. Amarna villa gardens had private chapels at the axis crossings. Temple gardens (Karnak, Hatshepsut's T-shaped pools) were sacred. Plant ordinary trees only: no goddess, chapel or shrine, and no T-shaped temple pool.

findings.element: Palms: date palm and doum palm silhouettes
findings.description: Date palm (Phoenix dactylifera): 15-25 m tall, one straight trunk covered in leaf bases (sometimes a clump), crown of 20-30 pinnate fronds 4-6 m long, crown 6-10 m across. Doum palm (Hyphaene thebaica): up to about 15-17 m, the trunk forks in two again and again, and each branch ends in a tuft of fan leaves about 1.2 x 1.8 m, with smooth dark grey bark. It grows along the Nile in Upper Egypt and Sudan. The forked doum is the most distinctively Nilotic tree silhouette.

findings.element: Enclosure walls: proportions, wavy courses, palace-façade niching
findings.description: Walls are mudbrick, and height is usually 2-3 times thickness (Abydos). Examples: Medinet Habu 18 m high and 10 m thick, Buhen 10 m and 5 m, Shunet el-Zebib 12 m and 5 m. From the Late Period on, temple enclosures used 'pan-bedding': wavy courses laid in alternating concave and convex panels, with a strong batter. It is associated with temple enclosures and read as the primeval waters, so treat it as temple architecture. The niched 'palace façade' (recessed panels, as on Shunet el-Zebib and at the base of the serekh sign O33) is a royal motif meaning the king's palace, and it suits a palace wall. Thick walls had timber and reed-mat layers every few courses.

findings.element: Serekh falcon
findings.description: The serekh (palace façade with the royal name) is usually topped by the Horus falcon, and some examples by the Seth animal. Use only the niched façade pattern, never the bird or animal on top.

findings.element: Giza pyramids as distant shapes: sizes, slopes, arrangement
findings.description: Khufu: originally 146.6 m tall on a 230.3 m base, slope 51.84 degrees (base about 1.57 x height). Khafre: 143.5 m tall on a 215.5 m base, slope 53.17 degrees. It stands on bedrock 10 m higher, so from most views it looks taller than Khufu, and it still keeps casing at its apex. Menkaure: 65.5 m tall on a 108.5 m base, slope 51.34 degrees. Three queens' pyramids stand to its south; the largest is about 25 m tall and the other two are small four-step pyramids. Khufu has three queens' pyramids on its east side. The big three stand a few hundred metres apart on a south-west diagonal, in descending size, about 9 km west of the Nile and 13 km south-west of central Cairo. They are royal tombs. As plain shapes they are allowed; the Sphinx, the valley and pyramid temples and the causeways are not.

findings.element: Pyramid colour and casing
findings.description: The casing was fine white Tura limestone, polished smooth. A surviving casing block is still bright, almost silvery. The exposed core today is a rougher brownish-yellow limestone. Khafre's lowest casing course was pink granite. Menkaure's lowest 16 courses (more than 20 m, about 30% of its height) were red Aswan granite. Gilded or electrum capstones are claimed but disputed: most capstones were plain stone. When finished, the pyramids would have stood out sharply, pale against the desert.

findings.element: Dahshur pyramids as a second skyline
findings.description: From Memphis, Dahshur lies on the same western horizon as Giza. Bent Pyramid: 104.7 m tall on a 189.4 m base. It rises at 54.5 degrees to the bend at 47 m (45% of its height), then at 43.4 degrees, a unique silhouette. Red Pyramid: 105 m tall on a 220 m base, 43.4 degrees throughout, so it looks low and broad. Both are plain shapes and could balance the Giza trio on the other side of the window.

findings.element: Aerial perspective (what makes a shape read as distant)
findings.description: With distance, contrast falls, detail blurs, saturation drops, and colour shifts toward the haze colour, and the horizon is palest. Value (lightness) matters more than hue. In dusty desert air, Mie scattering whitens the haze, so distant forms go warm pale grey or tan rather than blue. KovaaK's has no fog, so the effect must come from the material: pale, low-contrast and flat.

findings.element: Palace colour palette and courtyard floors
findings.description: Outside: whitewashed or white-stuccoed mudbrick (Malqata, Merenptah). Stone was kept for column bases, door frames, window slabs and pavements. The Palace of Apries stood on a massive platform, with limestone columns, pavements and wall cladding. Inside: red-brown wooden columns, blue, gold and red bands, yellow fields, blue-green faience tiles and inlays (daisies, persea, lotus, fish, birds), and gilded palm capitals. Floors were gypsum or white-stuccoed brick painted with pools and marshes, and stone pavement in the state areas (North Palace).

research.advice:
1) CONCEPT. Build the court in front of the palace front, as at Medinet Habu and Amarna. The player stands on the court floor. The existing window becomes the Window of Appearances, set as a projecting bay in a long, low palace front. Beyond the palace front, palms and pyramids show against the sky. The window and head stay the tallest and brightest things in view.

2) VIEW BUDGET (eye at (-6000, 0, 0); d = x + 6000).
- Screen size: +-51.5 degrees across and +-35.3 degrees up and down. At 1080p that is about 15 px per degree at the centre.
- The window covers +-24.5 degrees across (pilasters) and the lions reach +-30.9 degrees.
- Vertically the window runs from -16.7 degrees (sill) to +19.2 degrees (cornice); the head reaches +23.9 degrees.
- A floor at z = -900 enters the view at x = -4727 (the bottom edge of the screen). Its horizon is at eye level, which is the screen centre, behind the window.
- So the courtyard can only show in four places: the strip below the sill (-35 to -17 degrees), the two side bands (25 to 51.5 degrees on each side), and the sky.
- At the window line the view is only +-3750 wide. Side walls in front of the window are never seen, so don't build them.

3) TARGET SAFETY.
- Anything behind x = -2927 cannot cover a target.
- A flat floor at z = -900 is always safe.
- A raised item in the central strip in front must be at most about 900 - 870*d/3100 units above the floor: 535 at x = -4700, 480 at -4500, 340 at -4000, 200 at -3500, 85 at -3100.
- To also keep the lions in view, side items in front need |y| > 0.61*d.
- Run check_scene.py on all 13 layouts.

4) RECOMMENDED LAYOUT (about 15-25 objects; the budget is 60-120).
- (a) Floor: one block, x -4800 to -2600, y +-4400, top at z = -900.
- (b) Palace front: two wall blocks flanking the pilasters, from |y| = 1370 to 4400.
  - Set the face about 100-200 units behind the backdrop plane (x about -2800), so the window bay projects like Amarna's central terrace.
  - Put the top at z = +200 to +300 (1100-1200 above the floor, about 3-4.5 degrees up). That is above the horizon, so the wall hides the far ground and no huge distant floor is needed. A huge floor would also shimmer under a theme's grid texture at grazing angles.
- (c) Crown each wall with a limestone cavetto coping and a red-ochre bead, repeating the window's own cornice. For the thundah 'castle' feel, use a row of half-round 'Egyptian merlons' (Medinet Habu) instead, as one mesh per side. Optionally add niched palace-façade panels, with no falcon.
- (d) Foreground: a flush painted pool panel on the axis, after Malqata's pool-painted floor, at x -4400 to -3400 and y +-550. It needs almost no height: at most 5-10 units proud, with a thin limestone border. Its far edge sits about 5 degrees below the lowest targets and leads the eye to the window. Keep it calm (navy water). Low papyrus clumps at its near corners are optional; they must be 150 units tall or less at x < -4000.
- (e) Palms: plant them in the garden behind the wall (x about -2400 to 0), with crowns against the sky at 27-51 degrees across and 8-22 degrees up. For example: x = -2000, y = +-3000 to 4400, 2500-3800 units tall.
  - Date palms: one straight or slightly leaning trunk and 10-14 arching fronds, crown about a third of the height across.
  - Add one forked doum palm as the Nile signature.
  - Nothing may rise above the cornice within 26 degrees of the centre, so the head keeps its sky.
- (f) Pyramids rise from behind the wall, at a range of about 25k-35k.
  - Left gap, 28-44 degrees across: the Giza trio. A Khafre-like pyramid nearest the centre (slope 53.2, looks tallest), a Khufu-like one beside it (51.8), and Menkaure further out (51.3, about 45% of their height) with 1-3 tiny queens' pyramids.
  - Right gap: optionally the Dahshur pair, the Bent pyramid (54.5 degrees, then 43.4 degrees above 45% of its height) and the Red pyramid (43.4 degrees), for balance.
  - Size: apexes 8-10 degrees up (Menkaure about 5), so 4-6 degrees (60-120 px) show above the wall. Example: range 30000, 40 degrees across, 8 degrees up gives a centre at about (17000, -19300), a height of about 5100 above the floor and a base of about 8000.
  - Narrow each base by cos(angle across), about 0.77 at 40 degrees. The 103 FOV stretches side objects 1/cos wide (1.31x at 40 degrees), and uncorrected pyramids look squat.
  - The real Giza pyramids seen from a Memphite palace would be under 1 degree tall. This size is a deliberate exaggeration.
  - Make each pyramid one custom mesh (5 faces). QuadPyramid brushes exist but are uncalibrated.

5) MATERIAL SLOTS.
- Never reuse the g1 wall slot (the backdrop). The backdrop must stay unique.
- Floor and palace front: the free g1 ceiling slot in a mid grey clearly darker than the backdrop (e.g. PureColor 5a5d62, full-bright 0.3). This fits the user's grey preference, keeps the pale window the brightest element, and lets the navy lions read. Under any theme, all ceiling-type slots look alike, so the court then equals the window stone. The window then reads only by its navy outline, depth and shading, as it already does under Bassel 3.
- Pyramids and copings: g0 ceiling limestone. It is pale, which reads as far away and as Tura casing. Menkaure's red granite base band can use g0 ramp.
- Merlon and bead bands: g0 ramp (red ochre).
- Palms: dark umber silhouettes (g0 wall), in the same style as the stencil art. There is no green slot. The only way to get green is the Tree prop, which keeps its own colours under themes, but its look is unknown, so a sampler would be needed.
- Pool water: g1 ground (navy) for a calm look, or g0 ground (lapis) for a brighter one.
- Gold (g1 ramp): only if gilded palm capitals are added.

6) OPTIONAL SIDE PORTICOES (option B, more objects).
- Palm columns: height about 7.5 diameters, capital about a quarter of the height, abacus about 1 diameter, base disk about 2 diameters, 5 bands under the capital. Palace columns were red-brown wood with inlaid or gilded palm capitals.
- Columns placed in front of the window line near the screen edges fill the side bands and hide the pyramids. I'd use at most short colonnade stubs behind the ends of the palace front, kept under the wall top plus about 1000.

7) FLAGS TO RAISE WITH THE USER.
- Once any floor or wall exists, the lions' stencil holes show court, not sky. Sight lines through the lions hit the floor at x -2790 to -2210.
- The head keeps its sky as long as nothing near the centre rises above z of about 0.35*d.
- Brushes cast shadows. Check in game that no wall, palm or merlon shadow falls on the backdrop under the theme's sun: a dark patch behind black targets would hurt visibility.

8) BUILD AND TEST.
- Build it as one test scenario that replaces the Window Test (only one test installed at a time; retire the old one). Use DefaultNoCollision, keep every rotated piece inside meshes, and use groups 0 and 1 only.
- Report block counts and ask for an uncapped FPS check with no theme and with Bassel 3, against the Window Test's 616 and 474. Add palms and merlons in a second step only if there is headroom.
- Also confirm that the far pyramids render at about 20k-30k. The base map already draws a brush at x = -1,024,000, so this is probably fine.

9) LEAVE OUT.
- Religious: winged sun, uraeus or cobra friezes, vulture ceilings, the Aten disc and rays, Osirid colossi, offering scenes, altar courts and offering tables, the tree goddess, garden chapels and shrines, star ceilings, obelisks and flagstaff pylons, the sphinx, pyramid temples and causeways, the serekh falcon, ankh, djed and was.
- Also skip the captive motifs. They are political rather than religious, but violent.

findings.element: Who thundah is, and his castle scenarios
findings.description:
thundah uploads to the Workshop from the Steam account RATHERBEDEADTHANFAKE (steamcommunity.com/id/ifearthefuture). That account's own KovaaK's screenshot from 2024-06-03 highlights the row 'cAt thundah' as the account's own leaderboard entry. The KovaaK's Steam hub lists its uploads as 'RVNG thundah'. Two scenarios by this account have a castle.

(a) CastleTrack is a tracking scenario in the 'thundah Precise Tracking' Season 2 benchmark. The benchmark sheet's S2 tab lists thundahTrack, thundahRawControl, TrampolineTrack, CastleTrack, SkyTrack, LeafTrack, AngelTrack, TunnelTrack, CatTrack and OrbTrack. It was posted 2024-06-07, it is 138 KB, and kovaaks.com shows 4,995 plays. Its Workshop page (and the S3 versions) now says the item was removed. Its preview is the default thumbnail. No screenshot or video of it was found, and it is not on this PC. The user's stats hold no CastleTrack runs.

(b) Control Paradise was posted 2026-07-19 and updated 2026-08-24. It is a tracking scenario on the map 'Paradise Palace.json', and its Workshop preview shows a full castle. It is in the local Workshop cache. The user played it 22 times on 2026-07-21. So this is almost certainly the castle the user remembers. Related local thundah maps: IcyStrafes, PlazaStrafes and SnappyStrafes, each described as 'Original scenario by thundah'. The user has also played TrampolineTrack (S2) 8 times.

findings.element: thundah's castle (Control Paradise, 'Paradise Palace'): how it is composed and what frames the view
findings.description:
Sources: the Workshop preview image, which I viewed, and the map JSON. Units are map units at MapScale 2. The player's camera offset is 0 and the hitbox is tiny, so the eye sits on the SpawnPoint.

The player stands in the middle of a sunken square pool, about 2,180 x 2,240, in the centre of a paved courtyard. The courtyard is 8 slabs of 3,288 x 4,660, about 9,900 x 14,000 in all. An invisible Clip floor sits just above the water, and the eye is about 200 above the paving. The target moves about 1,328 ahead.

The view is one symmetric axis toward a keep:
- A crenellated curtain wall 1,470 tall, with merlons up to about 1,730. It stands 2,470-3,700 ahead, is about 3,900 wide, and is set as a shallow V.
- Two round flanking towers, 600 across and 2,270 tall, with 800-wide corbelled caps. They sit 1,800-2,600 ahead, 1,200-2,900 to each side.
- Behind them, a square keep block 2,240 wide, up to about 3,700, with pointed corner turrets. Its thin spires are cylinders 96 across and 800 tall.
- On the keep, a round tower 1,200 across that rises to about 6,800 with a 1,600-wide cap.

Lower raised ramparts, walls 4,320 long at 2,200-3,800 to each side, run from beside the player to the keep and converge in perspective. Four big corner towers stand 4,100-5,100 out to the sides: 1,008 across, 2,240 tall, with 1,200 caps and spires.

Angles from the eye: the keep wall top is at about 26 degrees and the merlons at about 34. The keep block (about 44 degrees) and the tall tower (about 56) run off the top of a 103-FOV screen. So what surrounds the targets is the wall and towers right behind them, the ramparts and towers cut off by the left and right screen edges, and the paving and pool at the bottom. In the preview, the pale sky fills roughly the upper third, but the preview camera sits further back and higher. From the real spawn, my rough render shows walls filling most of the frame and little sky.

The detail comes from repetition: 174 small blocks (80 x 140-200 x 140-200), turned in steps of -10, 20 and 38 degrees, are the merlons around the walls and round towers. The tiered towers are stacked cylinders of shrinking diameter (1,200, 800, 700, 600, 500, 400, 300).

findings.element: thundah's castle: materials, water, object count and the user's FPS
findings.description:
Materials: one material on all 8 slots, MI_WA_grid_8 grey 7f7f7f at full-bright 0.5. So the castle reads only through its silhouette, its shading and the grid lines, which is how the user's Bassel 3 theme (all four surface types alike) renders any map.

The map has no props. It has 273 drawn brushes: 216 Cube, 56 Cylinder and 1 Trim moulding. 223 of them are rotated. It also has 3 Clip brushes and 1 Water gameObject.

The Water object sets the pool's look: BaseColor 8398ff, DepthFadeColor 40dfbe, highlight and ripple colours, WaveSpeed 0 and WaveHeight 0. It is 10.5 x 10.5 x 0.08 at the basin centre, so its half-extent is about scale x 100.

The sky is not in the scenario. No header in any of the 390 installed scenarios has a sky, fog, sun or light key, so the theme sets the sky.

FPS: the user's 22 runs on 2026-07-21 averaged 359 FPS. That was the frame cap that day; every other scenario that day also shows 359. So the castle held the cap, but its exact cost is not known.

findings.element: Cockroach Simulator [with easter eggs]: the most detailed installed map
findings.description:
A giant-scale house interior; the player is the cockroach. MapScale 3.8125, 1,001 objects.

Brushes: 960, all drawn, no Clips. 830 are rotated. Meshes: 640 Cube, 97 Cylinder, 78 Torus, 46 Pipe, 43 WideCapsule, 27 RampConcave, 16 RampConvex, plus Pipe90, WedgeB, Cone and Tube.

Structure: floors are big slabs 64 thick (4,208 x 4,208 and 2,208 x 6,400). Walls are slabs 1,520 tall and 2,000-2,250 long, turned -90 degrees about x. The rest is furniture detail from hundreds of small repeated parts: 53 cubes of 20, 50 of 10, 49 small tori, 38 capsules and so on.

Props (25): Tree x7 at scale 1 and 4 (house plants), Crate x6, Window x6 stretched non-uniformly (1.2-2.3 x 0.5-4.1 x 2.5-3.4), Barrel x4, McCoy and TimmyButton.

The 15 targets are 2,800-6,500 from the player. 736 of the 985 drawn objects sit inside the forward view cone, most of them 1,500-20,000 away.

Materials: black PureColor wall, Paint_B floor, grey PureColor on g0 ceiling (full-bright 0.69, used on 2,524 faces), WoodFloorWalnut, MetalSheet, WoodParquet, BigConcreteTiles (full-bright 1) and red SciFiPaddingB.

FPS: the user's one run (2025-03-22) averaged 240. That day simple maps ran at 325-355, and a 40-brush VT Snake Track ran at about 245. That was old hardware and settings, so treat it as weak evidence that about 1,000 rotated brushes cost roughly 1 ms.

findings.element: Geometry Dash Lvl 1 - @wa11p1per
findings.description:
A side-scrolling obstacle course. MapScale 6, 791 objects.

Brushes: 525 drawn. 400 are DoubleRamps (10-20 unit spikes and steps) and 125 are Cubes. 475 are rotated and 7 have no collision.

findings.element: What our fixed camera can see (measured on the 13 built window layouts)
findings.description:
Screen: tanH is 1.2572 and tanV is 0.7072 (plus or minus 35.27 degrees).

The ground line is not z = -900. In Overflick the lion plinths and pilaster bases go down to z = -968: the lion mesh starts at -898 on 70-tall plinths. Across the 13 layouts, the lowest window brush ranges from about -856 (Pathing) to -1,129 (Early Braking, Early Click).

The window plus lions spans y plus or minus 1,584 (Speed Build) to plus or minus 2,223 (Pacing Drop, Slow Start). The top of the head ranges from 1,207 to 1,480.

The floor enters the bottom of the screen at d = floor depth / 0.7072. That is 1,210 to 1,597 in front of the eye (x about -4,790 to -4,403). So the floor band in front of the window fills the lower ~28-30% of the screen height.

At the window face (x = -3,020, d = 2,980), the screen spans y plus or minus 3,746 and up to z = +2,107.

Sky gaps:
- Beside the window: from yaw 28-37 degrees (depending on the layout) out to 51.5.
- Above it: from the cornice at about 19 degrees, or the head at 22-26, up to 35.3.

A side wall at |y| = W shows only where d > W/1.257. W = 2,500 appears from x = -4,011, and W = 3,000 from x = -3,614.

In front of the window, the no-go zone is each layout's opening, which already includes the 60 margin and the parallax. An object there must be either:
- laterally outside |y| > s x d, with s from 0.26 (Speed Build) to 0.466 (Pacing Drop, Slow Start); or
- below the line from the eye to the opening's bottom edge. The maximum height above the floor is 430-527 at d = 2,000, 324-377 at d = 2,500 and 239-256 at d = 2,900.

A pool with a rim up to about 200 is therefore safe anywhere. Palms and columns must stand outside about 0.47 x d plus a margin.

The horizon (pitch 0) runs across the middle of the screen, through the target band's height. It can show only in the side gaps.

findings.element: Frame-time headroom
findings.description:
The Window Test reads 474 FPS under the user's theme, which is 2.11 ms. 400 FPS is 2.50 ms. So the whole courtyard has only about 0.39 ms before the cap. To stay 'well above 400', for example at 440 FPS (2.27 ms), leaves about 0.16 ms.

The detailed maps above prove little here, because each ran at the cap of its day. Control Paradise ran at 359 (273 brushes + Water), Surge at 442, IcyStrafes at 483, and Frog and Cata at 143. Only Cockroach (960 brushes) clearly ran below other maps.

The window's own 0.64 ms under the theme comes from 86 brushes. So cost depends on what the objects are (dense custom meshes, theme-painted area, shadows), not on the count alone.

findings.element: Palace court with columned porticoes (the Amarna model)
findings.description:
Egyptian palaces were organised around open courts reached through gateways, with colonnaded halls and porticoes around them.

At Amarna, the North Palace has two open courts divided by a pylon or a possible Window of Appearance, and its second court held a large basin or sunken garden. The Great Palace's 'harem quarter' had a sunken garden with a colonnaded hall along each long side.

This fits the user's pick. The window becomes the gateway at the end of the court, and porticoes of papyrus-bundle columns line the sides, lower than the gateway.

Avoid the Great Palace's court of colossal king statues in Osiris form. Those are religious (see the separate entry).

findings.element: Rectangular pool / sunken garden in the court
findings.description:
Palace gardens centred on a rectangular pond with fish and lotus. Rows of date palms and other trees stood around it, sometimes with a stair down one side and a colonnade or wall around. Such pools are sometimes read as images of the Nile marsh or the cosmos, but a plain pool carries no deity or cult sign.

The game supports this directly. Its Water gameObject has settable colours and can be set to no waves, as thundah does. A low limestone kerb (at most about 200 high) stays below every sightline.

Unknowns to test in game:
- whether themes repaint Water
- its FPS cost
- whether it reflects the black targets. A reflection would put decoy targets under the window.

findings.element: Date palms (and other garden trees)
findings.description:
Date palms lined palace and estate pools, which makes them a natural motif.

Some sources link the date palm to Re and the sycamore fig to Hathor. So use plain date palms without any added emblem, and prefer them to sycamores.

They can be built as one merged mesh each: a trunk of a few turned segments plus 8-10 frond blocks. The Tree or TallTree props are an alternative, but their look is unknown. Props keep their own colours under themes.

findings.element: Distant pyramids on the horizon
findings.description:
Pyramids are royal tombs, so they have a funerary meaning. The user allowed them as plain distant shapes: no gilded capstone, no temples, causeways or sphinx.

They must sit in the side gaps, about yaw 38-50 degrees, to clear the widest window at 37 degrees.

Example sizing:
- d = 20,000 with the apex 5 degrees above the horizon: height above the floor about 2,700, base about 4,300 at the Khufu slope of 51.8 degrees. It appears about 12 degrees wide.
- d = 35,000 with the apex at 4 degrees: height about 3,400, base about 5,400. It appears about 9 degrees wide.

They need a ground plane out to the horizon; otherwise sky shows below the horizon. Build them as one QuadPyramid brush each, or as one custom mesh for all.

findings.element: Items to avoid from palace and gateway research
findings.description:
The colossal king statues in Osiris form in the Amarna Great Palace court. Obelisks and temple flagstaffs. Sphinxes. The winged sun. Offering scenes.

Also keep plants to plain palms and papyrus: no Hathor-linked sycamore symbolism, and no lotus shown as a cult offering.

research.advice:
1. What to take from thundah's castle.
- Compose one symmetric axis. A dominant building sits right behind the targets; in our case that is the existing window, acting as the palace gateway.
- Lower side walls converge on it.
- Tall vertical accents at the left and right edges are cut off by the screen frame, like his corner towers.
- Paving and a pool fill the bottom, and sky fills the top.
- He uses one grey material for everything, so the castle reads through silhouette and shading. That is how the user's Bassel 3 theme will render our courtyard, so design for silhouette first.
- Do not copy his size or count (273 brushes, a whole 360-degree castle). Our camera never turns, so build only the view cone.

2. Build to our view cone.
- Floor: set the courtyard floor at each layout's window base. Measured, that ranges from about -856 (Pathing) to -1,129 (Early Braking), and is -968 in Overflick, not -900. Alternatively, use one fixed floor at about -1,130 and a stepped terrace under the window that absorbs the difference.
- The floor shows from about 1,200-1,600 in front of the eye up to the window, in the lower ~30% of the screen.
- Anything in front of the window must stay outside |y| > 0.47·d (the widest layout) plus a margin, or stay under about 250-500 above the floor, depending on distance.
- The side gaps run from yaw 37 to 51.5 degrees (widest layout) and are the only place the horizon shows.

3. A layout that fits the user's pick and the rules (about 15-30 objects).
- One paving brush on a ceiling-type slot. Use limestone g0 ceiling, because both ground slots are taken by lapis and navy.
- One huge desert ground brush (50-100k), so there is a horizon.
- A long pool on the axis in front of the window: 1 Water object with WaveSpeed and WaveHeight 0, plus 1 kerb mesh at most about 100 high.
- Two side porticoes as one merged mesh each: papyrus-bundle columns, architrave and cavetto coping. Keep their top below eye level (under about 900 above the floor), so the gateway stays dominant and the pyramids show above them.
- 2-3 plain pyramids at yaw 40-48 degrees and 20-40k away, with the apex 3-6 degrees above the horizon (QuadPyramid brushes or one mesh). Optionally 2-3 flattened capsules or spheres as dunes, the way Night Lantern and Surge build horizons.
- 2-4 date palms per side as one merged mesh each, placed so their crowns don't hide the lions or the pyramids.
- Keep the sky band above the cornice empty.
- For a colour without a theme, repaint the free g1 ceiling slot green for the palm fronds. Under themes everything turns grey, as it does in thundah's map.

4. Performance.
- Headroom under the theme is only about 0.16-0.39 ms (474 FPS now; 400 FPS is 2.5 ms), so build and measure in stages, and have the user measure FPS with and without Bassel 3 at each one:
  - (a) paving + ground + pyramids
  - (b) + Water
  - (c) + porticoes
  - (d) + palms
- Merge everything that doesn't need its own slot. Report object counts with each stage, as AGENTS.md asks.
- If the budget is short, the window's dense meshes are the known 0.64 ms and are the place to win time back.

5. Unknowns to test in a separate test scenario first. Keep material groups at 3 or fewer and one test installed at a time.
- Does Water reflect the black targets (decoy risk)? Is it repainted by themes? What does it cost?
- How do QuadPyramid faces take material slots?
- Does a 100k ground brush behave?
- What do Tree, TallTree, LandscapeB and Rock* look like? Only a small sampler and the user's eyes can settle this; LandscapeB could even serve as a desert backdrop.
- check_scene.py checks brushes and props but likely not the Water gameObject. The pool is at floor level, so it is safe anyway.

6. Keep to the rules. No obelisks, flagstaffs, sphinxes, Osiride colossi, winged sun or temple buildings. The pyramids stay plain, distant shapes. The courtyard is a palace court (Amarna North Palace: open courts divided by a gateway or Window of Appearance, with a basin garden), which carries no cult meaning.

designs.concept: Lean Court of Appearances. The player stands on the paved court of a palace. The existing window becomes the Window of Appearances: a pale limestone gate block set in a long, low, crenellated palace front of dark grey mudbrick-like wall. From the gate outward, each side has a short plain flanking wall behind its lion, then a shallow portico: red palm columns with gilded capitals, set in shadow under a flat roof, as at Amarna and Malqata. At each screen edge stands a battered corner tower with round 'Egyptian merlons' (the Medinet Habu migdol). The towers are cut off by the screen frame the way thundah's corner towers are, and that is the castle nod. A calm navy pool with a limestone kerb lies on the axis in the lower third and leads the eye to the gate (Malqata's pool floor). Beyond the wall, against the sky, a date palm (left) and a forked doum palm (right) flank the gate. The Giza trio rises on the left and a Dahshur pair on the right, at 36-43 degrees across, as plain distant shapes whose bases are hidden by the wall. Everything is a few large pieces: 15 objects, and no props. The head stays the tallest thing on screen (v 0.447 in tan-space; towers 0.368, cornice 0.360, palms 0.381, pyramids 0.18-0.25, wall crenellations 0.12-0.135). The sky above the cornice stays empty. All geometry is relative to zf, the layout's window base (the lowest window brush: -968 in Overflick, -957 to -1129 across the 13). The palms and portico length adapt to each window's width.

designs.theme_notes:
Surface types:
- Wall: palace, towers, palms, sign outlines, backdrop.
- Ceiling: window stone, paving, kerb, crowns, pyramids.
- Ramp: column shafts and capitals, bands.
- Floor: pool, lion bodies, signs.

Under the 105 themes where wall differs from ceiling, the palace front stands apart from the gate and the paving. The columns differ from the back wall in 96 themes, and the pool from the paving in 79.

Every element of the skyline reads under every theme, because themes set the sky separately. That covers the crenellations, the tower tops, the palms, the pyramids and the head. The design is silhouette-first, as thundah's one-material castle is.

Bassel 3, read from its file:
- MARBLE POLISHED on all four types.
- Wall type at full-bright 0.76 with texture scale 0.1.
- Floor, ceiling and ramp at full-bright 1, which means flat and unshaded.
- Solid sky b3b4b6, sunVisible false.

Under Bassel 3, the paving, gate, columns, pool, lions and pyramids render flat white. Only the wall-type palace keeps some shading. See lean_view_bassel3.png:
- The gate and the columns read faintly against the palace.
- The lions read faintly against the flanking wall.

designs.concept: The design is the Court of the Window of Appearances, seen from the court floor. The existing window becomes the projecting central bay of a long, low palace front. The front's wall face is at x = -2800, so the bay stands 220 units proud of it. The front's limestone coping sits at an absolute z of +160, which is 2.9 degrees above the horizon, so the far ground never shows and no desert plane is needed. Open colonnades line both sides of the court. Each has red-brown palm columns with gilded capitals under a limestone architrave and cavetto cornice. The screen edge cuts the nearest column, and each row recedes to the palace front, so the stylobates, architraves and cornices form converging leading lines that point at the window. In the gap between each colonnade and the window, the horizon opens above the palace front: pale limestone pyramids stand low on it. The Giza trio is on the left; Djoser's step pyramid and the Red Pyramid are on the right. Two date palms on the right, and one date palm with one forked doum palm on the left, rise from the garden behind the palace front. They frame the upper corners as dark silhouettes, in the same spirit as the stencil head and lions. A calm lapis pool with a limestone kerb sits on the axis of the paved court and leads the eye to the window. The sky above the cornice stays empty, so the head keeps its sky. The window stays the tallest, brightest and most central element. For the "thundah castle" feel, the design borrows his composition (one axis, a dominant gateway, walls converging on it, tall accents cut off by the screen edges, silhouette-first under a one-material theme), not his object count. It uses 10 objects: 2 blocks and 8 custom meshes. That is deliberately far below the 60-120 budget, because the theme's cost seems to track object count (see risks). The floor level F is set per layout to the window's lowest stone: Overflick -968, Pathing -957, Early Braking -1129. Everything standing on the floor is measured from F, and the palace-front top and the pyramids use absolute heights. check_scene.py passed on all 13 layouts with the courtyard added. The test copies are in D:\Projects\flowfix\test_out\courtyard\check (not installed; the folder name may be shared with other concept runs).

designs.theme_notes:
What themes change:
- Themes repaint by surface type only. No props are used, so nothing escapes the repaint.
- The court paving and palace front are on the ceiling type, the same as the window stone. Under every theme they therefore take the same material as the window. The window then separates from its surroundings by depth (the bay stands 220 in front of the palace front), shading, shadows and its navy (floor-type) outline band, not by colour. That is the cost of the only free slot being ceiling type.

Themes that paint all four types alike (30 of 149, including Bassel 3; see atmos_view_bassel3.png):
- The court becomes one pale marble plaza, like thundah's single-grey castle, and reads by silhouette against the theme's sky.
- Palms, pyramid triangles, the colonnade columns and cornices, and the coping line all keep clear outlines against Bassel 3's grey sky (b3b4b6).
- In Bassel 3 the wall type has full-bright 0.76 and texture scale 0.1, against 1.0 and 1 for the other types. So the palms and the backdrop still shade a little and look slightly different from the stone.
- The pool, the lions and the signs vanish, exactly as the lions and signs already do today.
- Every added piece is solid geometry with depth (stylobate steps, the flared cornice, buttresses, the stepped pyramid), so it keeps some relief wherever full-bright is below 1.

Other theme groups:
- Floor differs from ceiling (79 themes): the pool shows as a panel of the theme's floor inside a stone kerb.
- Wall differs from ceiling (105 themes): the palms take the theme's wall paint and contrast with the stone colonnade and pyramids.
- Ramp is like ceiling in 116 themes: shafts and gold capitals merge into plain stone columns. The silhouette still carries them.

Sky:
- The theme sets the sky. 125 themes use preset skies with clouds, so the pyramids and palm crowns will sit against clouds there.
- The head's sky above the cornice is untouched, because nothing rises there within 26 degrees of the centre.

Without a theme, the default colours give the look in atmos_view.png:
- warm grey court, pale limestone, red and gold colonnades, blue pool, dark palm silhouettes, sand-pale pyramids;
- the palette follows real palace finishes: white or limestone stone, red-painted wooden columns, gilded capitals, blue water.

Stage C: add the palms and pyramids (10). At each stage the user reads uncapped FPS with no theme and with Bassel 3, against 616 and 474.

2) Crash safety.
- Custom meshes and big distant meshes change map structure, so try them in a separate test scenario first (crash-loop rule).
- Use groups 0 and 1 only, DefaultNoCollision, and the winding and MapScale rules in mechanics.md.
- The meshes at 20-33k range should render (the base map already draws a brush at x = -1,024,000), but confirm in game.

3) Target safety.
- check_scene.py passed on all 13 layouts: 89 objects in front of the targets checked, 0 overlaps.
- In front of the targets, only the floor, the pool (5 proud), the kerb (20 tall) and the colonnades are present.
- Closest approach on the wall plane: the stylobate projects to |y| 2393 and the far capital to 2670, against the widest envelope of ±1384 (Pacing Drop and Slow Start).

4) Lions.
- The colonnade stylobate projects just outside the widest lions (2393 against 2333), so they sit side by side in Pacing Drop and Slow Start.
- Once the palace front exists, the lions' stencil holes show court-grey wall instead of sky. Raise this with the user; they liked the stencil against the sky.

5) Layout variation.
- Floor F follows each layout's lowest stone. The research brief said Pathing's is -856, but the built Pathing map's lowest brush (lion plinths and pilaster bases) is at -957. So F runs from -957 to -1129 and eye height changes with it.
- The window cornice is wider in some layouts (up to 31 degrees), so how much of Khafre and the step pyramid it hides varies by layout.
- In Early Braking and Pacing Drop the doum crown comes within about 1 degree of the cornice corner. It stays at 29 degrees or more from the centre, outside the 26-degree head-sky rule.

6) Attention.
- The near-black umber palm crowns sit at least 29 degrees across and 15 degrees up; the saturated lapis pool sits at least 100 px below the lowest target. Neither is target-shaped, but either could pull the eye.
- Fallbacks: navy (g1 ground) for the pool, or a lighter palm slot. Also judge whether the gold capitals are too loud.

7) Shadows.
- The colonnades and palace front cast real shadows. Only the colonnades stand in front of the backdrop, at |y| 2470 or more, so only a very low side sun could shade the backdrop. Check under the theme's sun.

9) Historical licence and content rules.
- Real palace porticoes were roofed with back walls; these colonnades are open for the view.
- Pyramid sizes are exaggerated about 8x (true Giza from Memphis would be under 1 degree).
- No gods, winged sun, uraeus, ankh, djed, was, scarab, sphinx, obelisk, temple or causeway is used. The pyramids are plain distant shapes.
- Optional castle variant (not rendered): half-round "Egyptian merlons" on the palace-front coping. It would make the pyramid bases busier.

designs.concept: The court of a New Kingdom royal palace at Memphis, seen from the court floor looking west toward the pyramid field. The existing window becomes the Window of Appearances in a central bay that projects forward, as at the Amarna Great Palace. The bay sits in a long, low palace front. The front is a portico of eight palm columns in the Amarna and Malqata style: red-painted wooden shafts on round limestone bases, five gold binding bands and gilded nine-frond palm capitals. As at Medinet Habu, the window stands between the 4th and 5th columns. The columns carry a limestone architrave, a red torus bead and a three-step cavetto cornice like the window's own. Behind them is a whitewashed palace facade with two doors framed in red. The court floor is dark Nile-mud plaster. On the axis lies a calm rectangular pool with a 40-unit limestone kerb (Malqata's painted pool floor on the main axis, and the basin of the Amarna North Palace). Above the portico roofline (4.4 degrees up) there are three layers. The garden's date palms and a forked doum palm stand at the screen edges and are cut off by them. A mudbrick enclosure wall with rounded 'Egyptian merlons' (the Medinet Habu wall, Egypt's own castle) runs across the horizon. Above it show the tips of the pyramids a Memphite palace actually faced: Dahshur's Red and Bent pyramids on the left (south) and Giza's Menkaure, Khafre and Khufu on the right (north). They are white, because their Tura limestone casing was still in place in the New Kingdom. Every tall piece stands behind the backdrop plane. The head keeps its sky and the window stays the tallest and brightest thing in view. Nothing religious is used. There are 19 objects in all.

No theme (authentic_view.png): the pale window and grey backdrop are the brightest things on screen. The dark mud court fills the lower 24%. The colonnade reads red and gold against a whitewashed facade in shadow. Palms are near-black silhouettes at the edges, and the pale pyramid tips show above a dark merlon line.
Themes that paint surface types differently: the pavement, roof and enclosure (ceiling type) take the same paint as the window stone and the limestone trim. So the court looks like one stone with the window, and the window stands out through its navy outlines, depth and shading, as it already does. The pool (floor type) differs from the pavement in 79 of 149 themes. The column shafts and capitals (ramp type) differ from the ceiling-type facade in only 33 themes. The colonnade therefore reads mainly by silhouette against the facade, which sits in the roof's shadow (in my rough sun model the shadow covers nearly all of it). The palms and door openings are wall type and take the theme's backdrop paint. The palms stand against the sky, which themes set separately, so they read wherever the sky differs from the wall paint.
All-alike themes (30 of 149, including Bassel 3: MARBLE POLISHED, full-bright 0.76-1, solid grey sky; see authentic_view_alltheme.png): only silhouettes against the sky read. That means the skyline of palms, merlons, pyramid tips and the head, plus the portico's roofline and faint columns. The pool and pavement vanish into one grey plane. Target visibility: the court never overlaps the target envelope. Everything in front of x = -2918 is the flat floor and the pool with its 40-high kerb. I judged all 13 renders of the three concepts, then built, rendered and checked the merge.

1. Targets stay the clearest thing on screen.
- Only the floor, pool, kerb, stylobates, columns and portico roofs stand in front of the targets.

- The palms are mid-grey, not near-black the way atmos and authentic painted them, so no dark target-sized blob sits near the black targets.
- Every tall element is at least 26 degrees off-centre.

2. It reads at once as an Egyptian royal palace.
- Red palm columns with gilded capitals.
- A crenellated palace front with round "Egyptian merlons".
- Two migdol towers (the Medinet Habu gate towers, Egypt's own castle), cut off by the screen edge the way thundah's corner towers are. This is the castle nod the user asked for.
- A calm axial pool, and the Giza trio and two Dahshur pyramids rising above the merlons.

3. No religious symbols.

- 18 objects (10 blocks, 8 meshes) and 2,182-2,818 triangles (2,530 in Overflick). The window alone is 86 objects and about 13,000 triangles.
